title: Film & TV: The Big Picture
objective: After this level you can trace how still frames became movies and then television, and name the crafts that go into every film.
summary: A film is still photographs projected in rapid succession. Moving pictures ran from Muybridge's 1878 photos to the Lumières' 1895 show to TV, and every film draws on many crafts.

cards.headline: Nothing in a movie ever moves. Not one single frame.
cards.body: Pause any film and you're looking at a still picture. Britannica defines a film as a series of still photographs projected onto a screen in rapid succession, fast enough to look like smooth, continuous movement. Every chase and every kiss you've ever watched was a stack of stills in a hurry. This chapter follows how people turned that trick into cinema.

events.label: Eadweard Muybridge photographs a galloping horse with a row of cameras
The Lumière brothers project films for a paying audience in Paris
General Electric begins regular experimental TV broadcasts in the US

cards.headline: Television: moving pictures that come to you
cards.body: A film needs a projector, a screen and a room to sit in. Television takes a different road: it delivers moving images and sound electronically, from a source to a receiver. By 1928, General Electric was running regular experimental television broadcasts in the United States. Film gathered a crowd in front of one screen; television would send the pictures out to wherever the receivers were.

cards.headline: A film borrows from nearly every other art
cards.body: Britannica calls film exceedingly complex: it needs contributions from nearly all the other arts, plus countless technical skills such as sound recording, photography and optics. Writers, directors and actors shape the story; camera crews, costume and set designers shape the look; composers shape the sound. Then an editor trims and pieces the footage together, judging how long every shot should last. That's why the credits take so long to roll.

title: The Illusion of Motion
objective: After this level you can explain how a quick run of still pictures tricks the eye and brain into seeing smooth movement.
summary: Your brain supplies a film's motion: the phi phenomenon and beta movement turn quickly shown stills into movement. Persistence of vision is the older, oversimplified story.

cards.headline: A flipbook is lying to you, and your brain is in on it.
cards.body: Flip the pages and a doodle runs across the corner. Stop, and every page is frozen, each drawing just a little different from the last. The motion was never on the paper. So where does it come from? Not from your eyes clinging to each picture, as many books still claim. It comes from your brain.

cards.headline: A psychologist, a train and two blinking lights
cards.body: In 1912, psychologist Max Wertheimer described what he called the phi phenomenon. He reportedly noticed it on a train in 1910, when two railway signal lights flashing on and off in turn looked like one light moving back and forth. Nothing traveled between them. His brain supplied the trip. Show it two nearby things blinking one after the other, and it concludes that one thing moved.

cards.headline: Frames that shift a little each time
cards.body: Film leans on a close cousin, beta movement: a series of still images, each showing an object in a slightly different position. Run them quickly and you see the object move. Britannica credits the phi phenomenon and beta movement with making animation, film and electronic displays look continuous. Researchers go further: your visual system seemingly can't tell the motion in a movie from real motion.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: flicker fusion hides the flashing, apparent motion creates the movement. Two jobs, two effects.

cards.headline: Persistence of vision: the story that stuck around
cards.body: For almost a century, film books explained movies with persistence of vision: each image lingers on the retina and blends with the next. The trouble is that blended images would only pile up on top of each other, not move. Researchers now separate two effects. Flicker fusion makes flickering light look steady. Apparent motion turns still images into movement. Persistence of vision is the older, oversimplified story.

title: Frames per Second
objective: After this level you can explain what a frame rate is and why sound films settled on 24 frames every second.
summary: Frame rate counts frames per second. Hand-cranked silent films averaged 16 to 18; sound fixed 24 in 1927. Film shown faster than it was shot speeds up.

cards.headline: Why does everyone in an old silent film seem to be in such a hurry?
cards.body: Crowds scurry, cars zip, a chase looks like a wind-up toy. Before you blame the actors, count something: how many still frames pass every second. That one number, the frame rate, decides whether life on screen runs at the right speed.

cards.headline: Frames per second: the film's heartbeat
cards.body: A frame rate counts how many still frames a camera records, or a projector shows, each second. Your brain needs a fast enough stream: above about 15 frames per second, stills read as continuous movement. Silent-era cameras were mainly cranked by hand, averaging 16 to 18 frames a second, and silent films were photographed and projected at widely varying speeds.

cards.headline: Sound demanded a steady beat
cards.body: Talking pictures ended the guesswork. Sound made a standard speed necessary, and in 1927 it was fixed at 24 frames per second, which works out to 90 feet of 35 mm film a minute. In 1929 cameras were motorized to run at an even 24, so voices stayed in sync with moving lips. A hand crank can wobble. A soundtrack can't.

cards.fact: Shoot at 12 frames a second, show at 24, and life runs twice as fast.
cards.context: Film must be projected at the speed it was shot to look natural. Film something at 36 frames a second or more, show it at 24, and it plays slow and dreamy. Now picture a scene hand-cranked at 16 and projected at 24: everything moves one and a half times too fast. Hello, scurrying silent comedians.

title: Muybridge's Galloping Horse
objective: After this level you can explain how Eadweard Muybridge's row of cameras settled whether a galloping horse ever lifts all four hooves.
summary: In 1878 Muybridge's 12 thread-triggered cameras showed a galloping horse lifts all four hooves, legs tucked. His zoopraxiscope projected such images in succession.

cards.headline: Does a galloping horse ever fly? In 1878, a row of cameras answered.
cards.body: Watch a horse gallop and its legs become a blur. Does it ever have all four hooves off the ground at once? No eye was quick enough to say. So railroad magnate Leland Stanford hired photographer Eadweard Muybridge to prove that, for one moment, it does.

cards.headline: Twelve cameras and a mare named Sallie Gardner
cards.body: On June 19, 1878, at Stanford's track in Palo Alto, Muybridge lined up 12 cameras beside the course. As the mare Sallie Gardner galloped past, she broke threads attached to the shutters, and each camera fired in turn. Instead of one blur, he got a sequence: the gallop sliced into still moments, one after another.

cards.headline: Yes, but not the way painters drew it
cards.body: The photos showed all four hooves off the ground at once. Stanford was right. But the legs weren't stretched out front and back like a rocking horse, the way painters had shown galloping horses. They were tucked up under the horse's body. The camera saw what eyes had missed, and painters had been getting it wrong.

cards.headline: From proof to projection
cards.body: Muybridge then built the zoopraxiscope, a lantern that projected images in rapid succession onto a screen. Show his horse in sequence and it gallops again, an important step toward cinema. The catch: every sequence came from a whole row of cameras. A camera that recorded the sequence by itself, built in Edison's lab, would prove far more practical.

title: Edison's Peep Show
objective: After this level you can describe the Kinetoscope, the one-viewer movie cabinet built in Edison's lab, and why projection overtook it.
summary: Built mostly by W. K. L. Dickson in Edison's lab, the Kinetoscope showed films to one viewer through a peephole. Projection, serving a whole room, overtook it from 1895.

cards.headline: Before movie theaters, there were movie cabinets.
cards.body: Just a row of wooden cabinets. On April 14, 1894, the first Kinetoscope parlor opened in New York. You bent over a peephole and watched a film alone, while the next customer waited for a turn. How did movies begin as a show for one?

cards.headline: Built in Edison's lab, mostly by Dickson
cards.body: In February 1888 Muybridge visited Thomas Edison's lab and pitched a partnership; Edison passed. That October, Edison filed plans for a device to "do for the eye what the phonograph does for the ear" and called it the Kinetoscope. His assistant W. K. L. Dickson did the bulk of the experimenting, and most scholars give him the major credit. Their camera recorded the whole sequence by itself, no row of cameras needed.

cards.headline: Inside the cabinet
cards.body: The Kinetoscope was a wooden cabinet about four feet high. Inside, a loop of film about 50 feet long ran continuously past a lamp, while a spinning shutter let through flashes so brief that each frame seemed frozen. At that first parlor, 25 cents let you peer into five machines in a row, one film each.

cards.headline: Why the screen won
cards.body: One viewer per machine had a ceiling. Projected films could play to a whole room, so fewer machines served more paying viewers. Edison was slow to follow because peep shows were earning well, but in 1895 projection began to overtake them. In 1896 his company sold a projector, the Vitascope, as an Edison invention, though Thomas Armat and C. Francis Jenkins had built it.

title: The Lumières' First Screening
objective: After this level you can explain why the Lumière brothers' 1895 Paris show, films projected for a paying crowd, counts as cinema's birth.
summary: On December 28, 1895, the Lumières projected everyday-life films for a paying Paris audience, often called cinema's birth. The famous train panic is a legend.

cards.headline: Cinema has a birthday: December 28, 1895.
cards.body: That evening, at the Grand Café on the boulevard des Capucines in Paris, the Lumière brothers projected short films for people who had paid to get in. Britannica calls it the beginning of cinema history. But other inventors were already showing moving pictures. So why does this night get the candles?

cards.headline: From one peephole to a whole room
cards.body: The spark was Edison's Kinetoscope. After their father, Antoine, saw one in Paris in 1894, Louis and Auguste Lumière set out to show moving pictures to an audience instead of one viewer at a time. Their Cinématographe weighed under 5 kg and did three jobs in one box: camera, printer and projector. A film crew could carry it anywhere.

cards.headline: Why this show counts
cards.body: They weren't alone: in New York, Woodville Latham's Eidoloscope projector had gone public in April 1895, and the Lumières themselves first showed their machine to a small Paris audience on March 22, 1895. December 28 was their commercial premiere, projected films for a paying public. And from 1896 they sent trained camera operators to cities around the world to show films and shoot new ones. Cinema spread from that room outward.

mascot.line: Keep this: the train panic is a legend. A great story, with no evidence from the time.

cards.headline: The train that caused no stampede
cards.body: Their first films showed everyday French life: workers leaving the Lumière factory, a train arriving at a station. A famous story says that train sent audiences fleeing from their seats. Historian Martin Loiperdinger found no reports of panic from the time and calls the tale cinema's founding myth. The real wonder was quieter: ordinary life, moving, on a screen.

title: Méliès and the Trick Film
objective: After this level you can explain how Georges Méliès used stop tricks and staged scenes to make films of fantasy, like A Trip to the Moon.
summary: Magician Georges Méliès made the camera a magic box with the stop trick, which Edison's company had also used. His A Trip to the Moon (1902) helped make story films mainstream.

cards.headline: A magician saw the Lumières' machine and spotted a new kind of stage.
cards.body: Georges Méliès owned a Paris magic theater, the Théâtre Robert-Houdin. In December 1895 he saw the Lumière Cinématographe demonstrated. The Lumières pointed their camera at real life. Méliès would use it to make impossible things happen.

cards.headline: The bus that turned into a hearse
cards.body: By Méliès's own account, his camera jammed while he was filming in the Place de l'Opéra in Paris. When he projected the footage, a bus suddenly seemed to turn into a hearse. Stop the camera, change what's in front of it, start again, and on screen one thing transforms into another: the stop trick. He wasn't the first to use it. Edison's company had stopped a camera in 1895 to swap an actor for a dummy in a beheading scene.

cards.headline: A magic show, built for the camera
cards.body: Méliès turned the trick into a style. He built a glass-walled film studio at Montreuil, near Paris, and filled his films with stop motion, slow motion, dissolves, fade-outs, superimposition and double exposure. Where the Lumières caught a street as it was, Méliès made scenes that could only exist on film.

cards.fact: A Trip to the Moon (1902) crashes a spacecraft into the Moon's eye.
cards.context: Loosely adapted from Jules Verne, it runs about 14 minutes and uses stop motion and superimposition to make fantasy look real. It was one of the first films to be distributed internationally, and it helped make story films a mainstream product. Not bad for a trick born from a jammed camera.

title: The Great Train Robbery
objective: After this level you can explain how The Great Train Robbery of 1903 told a story by cutting between places.
summary: Porter's The Great Train Robbery (1903) told its story in 14 shots, cutting between places to show simultaneous action, and was shot partly on location.

cards.headline: In 1903, a 12-minute film jumped between places, and audiences kept up.
cards.body: Many films of the day were staged like a play seen from the front. The Great Train Robbery, made by Edwin S. Porter for Thomas Edison's company, cut from a telegraph office to a moving train and back again. Could an audience follow a story that jumped around like that?

cards.headline: Fourteen shots, one story
cards.body: The film is built from 14 separate shots. Bandits overpower a telegraph operator, rob a train's mail car and passengers, and flee with a posse on their trail. Porter cut back and forth between the tied-up operator and the bandits on the train, showing two things happening at the same time in different places. The cut became a bridge, not a break.

cards.headline: Out of the studio and onto the tracks
cards.body: Porter didn't keep everything on a stage. The film was shot in November 1903 at Edison's New York studio and on location in New Jersey, along a real railroad. Britannica calls it a dramatic departure from the front-facing, theatrical staging of its day, with the action continuing from shot to shot. Cut, and the story keeps going.

cards.headline: The shot aimed at you
cards.body: In one close-up, the outlaw leader, played by Justus D. Barnes, fires his pistol straight at the camera, which means straight at you. Exhibitors could show it at the start or the end of the film. The film's success tapped into fascination with the Old West and helped make the Western a staple of American movies.

title: How a Projector Works
objective: After this level you can explain how a projector's claw and shutter hold each frame still, then hide it while the film moves, so the picture never smears.
summary: A projector moves film intermittently, holding each frame still. A shutter hides each pull, and twin blades flash every frame twice: 48 flashes a second at 24 frames.

cards.headline: A projector stops the film 24 times a second, and hides every stop.
cards.body: If film slid smoothly past the lamp, each picture would smear into the next. So a projector does something stranger: it jerks the film forward, freezes it, shows it, and covers its tracks. Here's the stop-and-go machine behind every film screening.

cards.headline: Stop, show, pull, repeat
cards.body: The trick is called intermittent movement: the film advances one frame at a time, with pauses in between, so each frame stands perfectly still while it's shown. In cameras, a claw usually hooks the sprocket holes and pulls the film down. Many projectors use a Maltese cross, a four-slot wheel introduced in the 1890s that stops each frame in front of the opening, the aperture.

cards.headline: Borrowed from a sewing machine
cards.body: The Lumières' Cinématographe worked much like a sewing machine, which moves fabric forward and then holds it still for each stitch. A cam turned the crank's rotation into an up-and-down motion that drove claws through the film's perforations. Two turns of the crank each second advanced 16 frames, and each one paused to be shown.

mascot.line: Keep this: the claw moves the film, the shutter hides the move. Two parts, one smooth picture.

cards.headline: The shutter: a blink you never notice
cards.body: While the film is pulled down, a spinning shutter blocks the light, so you never see a frame move. But blinking dark 24 times a second would flicker, because flicker happens when images aren't flashed quickly enough to look continuously on. The fix: a twin-bladed shutter flashes each frame twice. At 24 frames per second, that's 48 flashes, and the screen looks steady.

cards.headline: Films saved as photographs on paper
cards.body: Film companies often copied each other's films. To protect its own, from October 1896 the Edison Company regularly registered films for copyright, sending them to the Library of Congress as photographic prints on paper rolls. The earliest surviving copyrighted film, a sneeze recorded on January 7, 1894, arrived as a series of photo prints. These paper prints form the Library's Paper Print Collection, and The Great Train Robbery is among them.

Muybridge sliced a gallop into stills; Edison's lab put film in a peephole box; the Lumières projected it for a paying crowd; Méliès made it magic; Porter cut it into a story. And a projector's intermittent movement holds each frame still, at the standard of 24 frames a second.

title: The Nickelodeon Boom
objective: After this level you can explain how five-cent storefront theaters made movies a cheap, everyday entertainment.
summary: Nickelodeons, storefront theaters charging a nickel, spread from Pittsburgh in 1905 to thousands by 1908, and film exchanges rented them a steady supply of films.

cards.headline: For a nickel, you could walk in off the street and watch the movies.
cards.body: In 1905 Harry Davis opened a nickelodeon in Pittsburgh: a movie theater named for its price, one nickel. It became the model for thousands more across the United States. Chapter 1 ended with films that could tell a story. This chapter starts with where people went to see them, and how cheap it was.

cards.headline: A theater in a shop front
cards.body: Nickelodeons were makeshift theaters in converted storefronts. For 5 to 10 cents you got about an hour's worth of short films, shown continuously with a piano playing along. What got them started? Britannica credits the popularity of The Great Train Robbery (Level 8) with encouraging investors to open these first permanent film theaters. A story film built the rooms that would show stories.

cards.headline: From a handful to thousands
cards.body: In 1904 the United States had only a handful of nickelodeons. By 1908 it had between 8,000 and 10,000. They were first identified with working-class audiences, then drew more middle-class viewers as the decade went on, and they became tied to the rising popularity of the story film.

cards.headline: Rent it, don't buy it
cards.body: Thousands of screens needed a steady supply of films. From about 1897 producers sold prints outright, so a theater had to buy every film it showed. Around 1903 Harry and Herbert Miles opened a film exchange in San Francisco: it bought prints from producers and leased them to theaters for a quarter of the purchase price. Renting made a fresh program affordable, and the exchange became the middleman between the people who made films and the people who showed them.

title: Why Hollywood?
objective: After this level you can explain why American filmmaking moved from the East Coast to Southern California in the 1910s.
summary: Filmmakers moved to Hollywood for its year-round sun, varied scenery and cheap land and labor; distance from the patent-pooling Trust is generally thought to have helped.

cards.headline: In 1911, Hollywood got its first studio. By 1915, it ran the show.
cards.body: A site on Sunset Boulevard became Hollywood's first film studio in 1911, and soon about 20 companies were making films nearby. By 1915 Hollywood was the center of the American film industry, with more than 60 percent of American production based there. Independent filmmakers had come all the way from the East Coast. Why?

cards.headline: The Trust
cards.body: In 1908 leading film companies, Edison's and Biograph among them, formed the Motion Picture Patents Company, known as the Trust. They pooled the key film patents and licensed them only to approved companies. They also had an exclusive deal with Eastman Kodak, so raw film stock went only to licensed producers. Anyone outside the Trust was an unlicensed independent, and the Trust meant to keep it that way.

cards.headline: Sunshine, scenery and cheap land
cards.body: Southern California had what a film crew needs. Its temperate climate allowed filming all year round. Within 50 miles of Hollywood lay a wide range of scenery, from mountains and forests to seacoast and desert. Taxes were low, and labor and land were cheap and plentiful. More films, shot faster, for less money.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: 'they fled the Trust' is the famous reason, but it's hedged. Sunshine, scenery and cheap land are the solid ones.

cards.headline: A continent away from the Trust
cards.body: It is generally thought that distance helped too: the Trust's headquarters was in New York City, on the other side of the country. The Trust didn't last. The US government sued it under the Sherman Antitrust Act, and it was formally dissolved in 1918. By then the independents had moved from the East Coast, and Hollywood had been the center of American filmmaking since 1915.

title: Alice Guy-Blaché
objective: After this level you can describe the career of Alice Guy-Blaché, one of the first directors to film made-up stories.
summary: Alice Guy, Léon Gaumont's secretary, made La Fée aux choux, one of the first story films, ran Gaumont's production, then founded Solax in America; much of her credit was later lost.

cards.headline: A company secretary directed one of cinema's first story films.
cards.body: Alice Guy was hired as Léon Gaumont's secretary in Paris. Then she directed a film of her own, La Fée aux choux (The Cabbage Fairy), which Britannica dates to 1896. How did she go from taking letters to making films, and why did history nearly misplace her?

cards.headline: A fairy tale, not a train
cards.body: The Lumières filmed everyday life: workers leaving a factory, a train arriving (Level 6). Guy filmed something made up. Britannica says she is generally acknowledged as the first director to film a narrative story, and many historians hold that her fairy tale came before Méliès's story films. A few historians date it as late as 1900, though. That's why 'one of the first' is the safe way to say it.

cards.headline: Running a studio's films
cards.body: Gaumont made Guy its head of production, and she directed nearly all of the company's films until 1905. She kept experimenting, too: from 1906 to 1907 she directed short sound films using Gaumont's Chronophone. The secretary had become the person deciding what the company put on screen.

cards.headline: Her own studio, then her name forgotten
cards.body: In 1907 Guy married cameraman Herbert Blaché and moved to the United States. In 1910 she founded the Solax Company, and by 1912 it had a new, state-of-the-art studio in Fort Lee, New Jersey. Yet many of her accomplishments were later forgotten or credited to male colleagues. After she returned to France in 1922, she couldn't find work in its film industry. The films outlasted the credit.

title: Griffith and The Birth of a Nation
objective: After this level you can explain how D. W. Griffith's film techniques shaped the feature film and why his most famous film is condemned for its racism.
summary: Griffith refined the close-up and cross-cutting over 400-plus Biograph films; his nearly three-hour The Birth of a Nation (1915) secured the feature film and glorified the Ku Klux Klan.

cards.headline: One film showed what movies could do, and did real harm.
cards.body: The Birth of a Nation came out in 1915 and ran nearly three hours, one of the longest films yet made. Its director, D. W. Griffith, is studied for how he told stories on film. The film itself is condemned for the story it told. This level holds both facts at once.

mascot.line: People mix this up all the time: Griffith refined these tools. Porter was already cross-cutting in 1903, back in Level 8.

cards.headline: Refined, not invented
cards.body: From 1908 to 1913 Griffith made more than 400 films for Biograph, mostly one-reelers. Along the way he introduced or refined the tools of film storytelling, including the close-up and cross-cutting, which edits together scenes in different places. He didn't invent cross-cutting: in 1903 Porter cut between a tied-up telegraph operator and the bandits on the train (Level 8). Griffith polished these tools over hundreds of films.

cards.headline: The feature film arrives
cards.body: The Birth of a Nation was adapted from Thomas Dixon's 1905 novel The Clansman. It used special effects, jump cuts and facial close-ups, and Britannica says it secured the future of feature-length films and the acceptance of film as a serious medium. After it, a movie could fill an evening.

cards.headline: What the film says
cards.body: The film is openly racist. Its second part, set during Reconstruction, portrays Black people as unworthy of freedom and the vote, and shows the Ku Klux Klan as heroes restoring order. Black characters such as Gus were played by white actors in blackface.

cards.headline: Protest and harm
cards.body: Protests, mainly organized by the NAACP, met the film from its 1915 premiere, and showings were stopped in a few states and cities. In late 1915 the Ku Klux Klan was revived in Georgia, directly inspired by the film. Griffith responded to his critics with Intolerance (1916), a film about intolerance and censorship.

title: Silent Comedy
objective: After this level you can explain how Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton built comedy out of timing, stunts and pure movement.
summary: Chaplin's Tramp mixed slapstick with poignancy, and Keaton, the Great Stone Face, built comedy from deadpan timing and dangerous stunts such as Steamboat Bill, Jr.'s falling house front.

cards.headline: Silent comedy's most famous stunt: standing perfectly still.
cards.body: In Steamboat Bill, Jr. (1928), the front of a house falls toward Buster Keaton. He doesn't move. The open attic window lands exactly around him, on a spot marked with a nail. Had he moved, he would have been crushed. With no voices to lean on, silent comedians got their laughs from timing, stunts and pure movement.

cards.headline: The Tramp gets dressed
cards.body: Charlie Chaplin was touring America with the Karno company in 1913 when he was signed for Mack Sennett's Keystone comedies. In Kid Auto Races at Venice (1914) he first appeared as the Tramp: too-small coat, too-large pants, floppy shoes, a battered derby, a small mustache and a cane. You could read the character from the back row before he did a thing.

cards.headline: A laugh with a lump in your throat
cards.body: Chaplin blended physical comedy with poignancy. In The Gold Rush (1925), the Tramp must eat his shoe to stay alive: a gag and a hardship in one scene. He became his own director, and in 1919 he cofounded United Artists with Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks and D. W. Griffith.

cards.headline: The Great Stone Face
cards.body: Keaton grew up in his family's vaudeville act, the Three Keatons, doing knockabout acrobatics, and learned early to take a fall without getting hurt. On film he became the Great Stone Face, performing death-defying stunts without a smile. In The General, a Civil War comedy, he staged most of the action in and around trains. He said the more serious he turned, the bigger the laugh.

title: A Night at the Silent Movies
objective: After this level you can describe how silent films were shown, with intertitles, live music and grand movie palaces.
summary: Silent films were shown with intertitles for dialogue, live music from pianists, organs or orchestras guided by cue sheets, and from 1914 in huge movie palaces like the Strand.

cards.headline: Silent movies were almost never silent.
cards.body: No voices came from the screen, but the room was rarely quiet. Silent films were almost always shown with live music, and in the grandest theaters around 3,000 people watched together. Here's how a night at the silent movies worked.

cards.headline: Words between the pictures
cards.body: When a character needed to speak, or the audience needed to know where and when, the film cut to a printed card: an intertitle. Filmmakers used them for dialogue or explanation. Some directors tried to do without. F. W. Murnau's The Last Laugh (1924) told its story almost entirely without intertitles. The pictures had to do the talking.

cards.headline: Music in the room
cards.body: Early screenings usually had a solo pianist, often improvising. Larger theaters used organists or whole orchestras. Films were eventually sent out with published cue sheets suggesting what the pianist or organist should play. Cue sheets gave accompanists a plan for each film.

cards.headline: Palaces for pictures
cards.body: In 1914 New York's Strand Theatre opened as the first of the 'dream palaces': huge movie theaters with luxurious interiors. It seated around 3,000 people. Big films got big sound: The Birth of a Nation was shown with an orchestra playing Joseph Carl Breil's score, compiled from many sources. Pittsburgh's nickel storefront had opened in 1905. In nine years, movies had moved into palaces.

title: German Expressionism
objective: After this level you can explain how films like The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari used twisted sets and deep shadows to show inner terror.
summary: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari used deformed sets and painted light and shadow to show a narrator's tortured mind, and gave rise to German Expressionism, including Murnau's Nosferatu.

cards.headline: What if the scenery were as frightened as the hero?
cards.body: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, directed by Robert Wiene in postwar Germany, tells of murders committed by a sleepwalker at the bidding of a demented showman. But the most famous thing in it isn't a character. It's the town: warped, jagged, with light and shadow painted on. Why build a world that looks wrong on purpose?

cards.headline: Sets that show a state of mind
cards.body: The story is told by a narrator in a tortured state of mind, and the film shows you his mind instead of the real world. Wiene hired three Expressionist artists to design sets with exaggerated dimensions and deformed spatial relationships. Nothing is the right size or at the right angle. You don't just watch the fear. You walk around inside it.

cards.headline: Shadows made of paint
cards.body: Even the light is fake. Patterns of light and shadow were painted straight onto the scenery, and even onto the characters' makeup. It heightened the style, and it also saved electric power, which was rationed in postwar Germany. A shortage became a signature look.

cards.headline: A movement is born
cards.body: By turning disturbed states of mind into décor, Caligari greatly influenced the German UFA films that followed and gave rise to the movement called German Expressionism. One of its classics is F. W. Murnau's Nosferatu (1922), an unauthorized adaptation of Bram Stoker's Dracula. Murnau also made The Last Laugh (Level 16), which barely needed intertitles.

title: Soviet Montage
objective: After this level you can explain how Sergei Eisenstein cut shots against each other to stir an audience, as in Battleship Potemkin.
summary: Short of film stock, Soviet filmmakers made editing the heart of cinema; Eisenstein held that colliding shots create meaning, as in the Odessa Steps of Battleship Potemkin (1925).

cards.headline: A country short of film taught the world how to cut it.
cards.body: After the Russian Revolution, a foreign blockade left Soviet filmmakers short of equipment and film stock. By 1925 Sergei Eisenstein's Battleship Potemkin showed what they had learned: the cut between two shots could hit an audience like a punch.

cards.headline: Film as a priority
cards.body: Lenin recognized film's power as propaganda and its ability to communicate quickly, and his government gave top priority to building the Soviet film industry. The state film school in Moscow, later known as VGIK, was the first film school in the world. But the blockade stopped imports of equipment and stock, which the country couldn't yet make itself, and power shortages limited the rest. Every foot of film counted.

cards.headline: Learning from Griffith
cards.body: Teacher Lev Kuleshov had a print of Griffith's Intolerance (Level 14), and he screened it for his workshop students until they had memorized how its shots were put together. Soviet filmmakers held that time and space in a film must bow to editing, which they called montage, from the French verb monter, 'to assemble'.

cards.headline: Shots that collide
cards.body: Eisenstein went further. He believed meaning in a film comes from the collision of opposing shots: put two clashing images side by side, and a new idea sparks between them. He compared it to the explosions of an internal combustion engine, each one driving the film forward.

cards.headline: The Odessa Steps
cards.body: Battleship Potemkin (1925) was commissioned for the 20th anniversary of the 1905 Revolution and dramatizes a mutiny by the ship's sailors. Its 'Odessa Steps' sequence, in which soldiers massacre citizens on a stone staircase, is one of the most famous sequences in film history. Cut from clashing shots, the slaughter takes on symbolic meaning.

title: Nanook and the First Documentaries
objective: After this level you can explain what Nanook of the North set out to show and why some of its scenes were staged.
summary: Flaherty's Nanook of the North (1922) showed Inuit life but staged much of it: a cut-away igloo, a staged seal hunt, a borrowed family and harpoons instead of rifles.

cards.headline: An early documentary classic filmed a house with a wall missing.
cards.body: Robert Flaherty's Nanook of the North (1922) set out to show Inuit life in the Canadian Arctic, and it became an international success. It also has a puzzle at its heart: much of what it shows was arranged for the camera. Can a film be real and staged at once?

cards.headline: Filming at Inukjuak
cards.body: Flaherty arrived at Port Harrison, now Inukjuak, in northern Quebec, in August 1920. For his lead he chose Allakariallak, the best hunter in the district, who played 'Nanook'. Britannica calls the result a dramatic interpretation of Inuit life: real people and real skills, shaped into a story.

cards.headline: Arranged for the camera
cards.body: A camera and its operator couldn't fit inside a real igloo, so a second igloo was built with a wall removed. The two women shown as Nanook's wives weren't his wives, and the two children weren't his. Look closely at the cuts in the famous seal hunt, and you can tell it was staged too.

mascot.line: Keep this: staged doesn't mean invented. Nanook shows real people and real skills, arranged and reenacted for the camera.

cards.headline: Yesterday, performed today
cards.body: By 1920 Inuit hunters used rifles. Flaherty had his subjects hunt with harpoons and spears instead, to show an older way of life. The Lumières had filmed what was in front of them (Level 6). Flaherty rebuilt the past and filmed that.

cards.headline: A new word
cards.body: Flaherty is often called the father of the documentary film. The word itself arrived a few years later: John Grierson first used the term documentary about Flaherty's film Moana (1926).

title: From Script to Screen
objective: After this level you can name the five stages of making a film, from development to distribution, and what happens in each.
summary: A film moves through five stages: development, pre-production, production, post-production and distribution. The shoot is often the shortest.

cards.headline: The cameras roll for a few weeks. The film takes far longer.
cards.body: Picture moviemaking and you probably see a busy set. Yet Britannica notes that the shooting phase usually lasts just a few weeks. Most of a film's life happens before and after it. Let's follow one film from an idea all the way to an audience.

cards.headline: Development: an idea, a script and the money
cards.body: Britannica traces a film's journey as a value chain, from choosing an idea to someone watching the result in a theater or on TV. It starts in development. A producer picks an original idea or buys the rights to an existing story: a novel, a comic book, a play or a game. A writer develops a screenplay, the producer estimates the costs, then goes looking for money.

cards.headline: Pre-production and production: plan it, then shoot it
cards.body: With money found, pre-production begins. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics lists its work: developing the script, auditioning actors and planning how each scene will be shot. Then comes production, the shoot itself. Britannica calls it delicate and expensive, because it needs many people working at the same time.

cards.headline: Post-production and distribution: finish it, then share it
cards.body: Post-production is likely to last longer than the shoot. Picture and sound are edited, effects and titles are created, music and sound effects are added, and everything is combined. The result, a master copy, is sold to a distributor that makes copies for release in theaters. Five stages: develop, prepare, shoot, finish, distribute.

title: The Screenplay
objective: After this level you can explain how a screenplay is laid out and why one page is reckoned at about one minute of screen time.
summary: Each scene in a screenplay opens with a capitalized INT. or EXT. heading. A standard Courier format makes one page about one minute of screen time.

cards.headline: You can time a movie by counting paper.
cards.body: Pick up a screenplay and check the last page number. Screenwriting teacher Syd Field called it a good rule of thumb: one page of screenplay is about one minute of screen time. How can a stack of paper keep time?

cards.headline: Every scene starts with an address
cards.body: Britannica defines a screenplay as the written text a film production is built on. Each scene opens with a scene heading, or slug line, in capitals and usually starting with INT. or EXT.: inside or outside. It also names the place and the time of day. Below come action lines describing what the audience will see, then each speaker's name in capitals with the dialogue beneath.

cards.headline: One typewriter font for everyone
cards.body: The Academy's Nicholl Fellowships format guide calls Courier, 12-point, the industry standard, and says to steer clear of other fonts. Courier comes from the typewriter era, and each of its characters takes up the same amount of space. Add standard margins and spacing, and every writer's page is built the same way.

mascot.line: Keep this: a page works as a clock only because every page is built the same way. Same font, same margins, about a minute.

cards.headline: Why a page is about a minute
cards.body: Because every page is built the same way, the page count works like a clock. Field says the rule holds whether a script is all action, all dialogue or a mix. Studios and producers use it to estimate budgets and shooting schedules. It's an estimate, not a law: one short line of action can play for minutes, and rapid-fire dialogue often runs faster.

title: Storyboards and Shot Lists
objective: After this level you can explain how storyboards and shot lists plan a scene before a camera rolls.
summary: A storyboard draws a film shot by shot, a method the Disney studio pioneered; a shot list tracks every shot the crew must capture.

cards.headline: A film can be drawn, shot by shot, before a camera rolls.
cards.body: Filmmakers plan scenes on paper long before the shoot. Two documents do most of the work: a storyboard, which shows what each shot will look like, and a shot list, which keeps track of every shot the crew needs to film.

cards.headline: The storyboard: your film as a comic strip
cards.body: ACMI, a museum of screen culture in Melbourne, calls a storyboard a shot-by-shot visual plan that shows what a film will look like before it's shot. Each panel stands for one camera shot, and the board guides the team doing the filming. You don't draw every frame, and it needn't be art: stick figures will do, as long as the shot type and what's in it are clear.

cards.headline: A tool that grew up in animation
cards.body: The Walt Disney Family Museum says the Walt Disney Studios pioneered storyboarding. A storyboard maps out a story in a series of sketches, so filmmakers can see the plot in sequence and judge whether the story is clear. Laid out like that, plot holes and other inconsistencies are easier to spot.

cards.body: A shot list keeps track of all your shots, ACMI explains, so when filming day comes you know exactly what you need to film. It can note each shot's camera movement, even when the answer is 'static', meaning the camera doesn't move. On set, filmmakers often keep the storyboard and script at hand too, to set up shots the way they planned.

title: Who Does What on a Film Set
objective: After this level you can explain the jobs of the director, producer, cinematographer, gaffer, grip and script supervisor.
summary: The producer runs the money, the director the vision, the cinematographer the camera, the gaffer and grips the light, and the script supervisor continuity.

cards.headline: The campfire in a movie scene might be nothing but lights.
cards.body: When a scene calls for a campfire that can't really be built on set, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics explains, gaffers use lights to recreate a fire's flicker. That's one job among many. A film set runs on specialists, so here's who does what.

cards.headline: Producer and director: the business and the vision
cards.body: Producers are a film's managers, from securing the money in pre-production to approving the finished film. They hire the director, create the budget and approve changes to the script, budget or schedule. The director develops the film's artistic vision: helping choose the cast, overseeing the shooting of each scene, guiding the actors and working closely with the cinematographer.

cards.headline: Camera and light: cinematographer, gaffer, grip
cards.body: The cinematographer, also called the director of photography, is in charge of shooting the scenes and decides how the camera moves to serve the director's vision. The AFI adds that they choose the camera, the lenses and how to light each scene. The gaffer, the chief electrician, designs and adjusts each scene's lighting scheme. Grips carry out that lighting plan and can support the camera on a dolly or crane.

cards.headline: The script supervisor: keeper of continuity
cards.body: A film is shot take after take, and the pieces must fit when they're cut together. The script supervisor keeps the record: slate numbers, notes on each take, lenses, the action and running times, plus props, makeup and costumes. The BFI calls continuity something that, by its nature, should be entirely invisible. If you never notice it, it worked.

title: Shot Sizes
objective: After this level you can tell a wide shot, a medium shot and a close-up apart and say what each one is good for.
summary: Shot sizes are named by how close the camera is: a wide shot shows the whole body and setting, a medium shot the waist up, a close-up the face and its emotion.

cards.headline: Same actor, same moment, three different feelings.
cards.body: Where you put the camera changes what the audience notices. ACMI explains that filmmakers sort shots by one measure: how close the camera is to its subject, whether that's a character, a setting or an object.

Yale's Film Analysis guide adds that extreme long shots are usually the first or last shots of a sequence. A long shot also shows a whole body moving, which is why it's common in Hollywood musicals and 1970s martial arts films.

cards.headline: Close-ups pull you into a feeling

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics gives a cinematographer's example: to draw the audience into a key scene, shoot the actors' faces at close range. Sizes are relative, though. title: Camera Angles
objective: After this level you can explain how high, low and tilted camera angles change how powerful or uneasy a character seems.
summary: Most shots sit at eye level. A low angle can make a character look strong or menacing, a high angle small or weak, and a Dutch angle suggests unease.

cards.headline: Lower the camera and a character grows. Raise it and they shrink.
cards.body: Most shots are taken from eye level, ACMI explains, because it's easy and it's the natural way you see people. Leave that line, and the angle starts to say something about the character.

cards.headline: Low angle, high angle
cards.body: In a low-angle shot the camera sits well below eye level, looking up. That can make a character look heroic and strong or, aimed at a villain, scary and intimidating. A high angle does the opposite: the camera is above the character, angled down, which can make them look small and weak. Same actor, same line; the camera's position changes how you read them.

mascot.line: Don't memorize 'low means strong' as a law. Ask what the angle does in this scene: an angle suggests, it doesn't dictate.

cards.headline: One family, two angles
cards.body: Yale's Film Analysis guide points to The Color of Paradise, a 1999 Iranian film by Majid Majidi. The father, who rules his family, is often shot from a low angle, which enlarges him. His blind son Mohammad and elderly grandmother are often shot from a high angle, stressing their dependence and smallness. Yale adds that such readings aren't fixed: that view from above may also suggest God watching over them.

cards.headline: Tilt the frame, tilt the world
cards.body: Tip the camera so the frame isn't level and you get a canted framing, also called a Dutch angle. Yale says it creates an impression of chaos and instability. ACMI adds that it's often used when a character is going through something unusual or distressing, so the audience feels that something isn't right.

title: Moving the Camera
objective: After this level you can explain how pans, tilts, dolly shots, crane shots and handheld shots move a viewer through a scene.
summary: Pans and tilts turn the camera in place; dollies, cranes and handheld shots move it through the scene; a zoom only enlarges part of the picture.

cards.headline: A camera can turn its head, take a walk or fly.
cards.body: So far the camera has held still while we chose its size and angle. Britannica describes camera movement as moving the camera during shooting to change the framing, scale and angle. Each kind of move gives you a different ride through a scene.

cards.headline: Pan and tilt: turning in place
cards.body: A pan turns the camera horizontally, left or right; the word comes from panorama. It can follow a character or reveal something the audience hasn't seen yet. A tilt swivels the camera up or down. Start at a building's base and tilt up to the top, and you feel its height. In both moves the camera turns but doesn't travel.

cards.headline: Dolly and crane: the camera travels
cards.body: In a tracking shot the camera itself travels forward, backward or sideways. Often it rides a dolly, which the AFI defines as a small wheeled platform that runs on track or is moved by hand; on rough ground, rails like train tracks are laid. A crane, a large arm, carries the camera through the air, and Yale says crane shots can make you feel you see everything. Level 24's grips support both.

cards.headline: Moving isn't zooming
cards.body: A zoom can look like a move, but it isn't one. When the camera dollies, its distance to each object changes, so the spacing between things in the frame shifts. A zoom only changes the lens's focal length. It enlarges part of the picture without changing perspective, which gives it a flat look.

cards.headline: Handheld: the camera breathes
cards.body: In handheld shooting the operator's own body supports the camera. Yale traces the style to newsreel and wartime camera operators with small cameras, later taken up by documentary makers. It's cheap and feels spontaneous, but jerky. Gyroscopic Steadicams, from the 1970s, let operators make smooth moving shots without bulky equipment.

title: Lenses and Focus
objective: After this level you can explain how a lens's focal length and depth of field decide what looks near, far, sharp or soft.
summary: Wide-angle lenses stretch depth and telephotos squeeze it, though camera distance does the real work; depth of field decides how much of the image is sharp.

cards.headline: Two lenses can make the same walk look fast or slow.
cards.body: Film a person walking toward the camera. With a wide-angle lens they seem to approach quickly; with a telephoto they seem to barely get closer. Nobody changed speed. So what changed?

cards.headline: Focal length: wide, normal and long
cards.body: A normal lens shows perspective close to what your eye sees; for 35 mm film that's a 50 mm lens. Shorter lenses are wide-angle and let more space into the frame, handy in a real room. Lenses two or more times longer are telephoto. A wide-angle lens exaggerates depth, stretching near and far apart; a telephoto compresses it.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: the lens gets the credit, but distance does the squeezing. The lens picks how much you see.

cards.headline: The catch: where the camera stands
cards.body: The cinematography guide by Kris Malkiewicz and M. David Mullen adds a twist. Perspective really depends on the distance from camera to subject, not on the lens. From the same spot, different lenses change how much you see, not the perspective. A telephoto shot is almost always taken from farther away, and that distance is what squeezes the depth.

cards.headline: Depth of field: how much is sharp
cards.body: Depth of field is how far, from near to far, the image stays in sharp focus. Bright light, a narrow aperture and a wide-angle lens all give more of it. Shrink it to shallow focus and only one plane stays sharp, which pulls your eye to what matters without a cut. Yale's guide notes shallow focus is very common in close-ups.

cards.headline: Rack focus: moving your eye for you
cards.body: Focus can also change during a shot. In a rack focus, one plane slides out of focus as another comes in, steering your attention and linking two people or objects in the same frame.

title: Lighting a Scene
objective: After this level you can explain three-point lighting and how high-key and low-key lighting set a mood.
summary: Three-point lighting uses a key, a fill and a backlight. Raise the fill for bright high-key scenes; drop it for shadowy low-key ones.

cards.headline: Most mainstream films light a face from three directions.
cards.body: Britannica says lighting helps set the tone of a scene and emphasize the parts that matter. Yale's Film Analysis guide calls three-point lighting the standard scheme of classical narrative cinema. Learn its three lights, then watch one of them change the mood.

cards.headline: Key, fill and back
cards.body: The key light is the bright main light on the actor. A fill light from the opposite side softens the shadows the key casts, so they stay faint. A backlight, behind the actor, picks them out from the background. Together the three give a face a sense of depth. Documentaries and realist films often skip the setup and use natural light, for a sense of authenticity.

cards.headline: Fill turned up: high-key
cards.body: In high-key lighting the fill is raised almost to the level of the key. The picture comes out bright, with few shadows on the main characters. Yale ties it to entertainment genres such as musicals and comedies.

cards.headline: Fill turned down: low-key
cards.body: Low-key lighting uses very little fill. The result is strong contrast between bright and dark, with shadows that hide parts of the characters. Yale links it to suspense genres such as film noir. Same three lights, very different mood, and the fill makes the difference.

title: Checkpoint: Shooting a Scene
objective: After this level you can explain how planning, crew, camera and light work together to capture a single scene.
summary: The clapperboard labels each take and marks one instant on picture and sound. The chapter traced a scene from script and plan to crew, camera and light.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: every take begins with a snap.
cards.body: Just before a take, someone holds a board up in the camera's view and claps it shut. That small ritual ties together the plan, the crew and the camera from this whole chapter. Here's what it does, then the chapter in one breath.

mascot.line: It connects: the slate numbers on this board are what Level 24's script supervisor writes down, take after take.

cards.headline: The clapper: a label and a sound
cards.body: Britannica describes the clapper, or clapperboard: a slate showing information about the take, topped by a hinged arm. Its wooden jaws, about a foot long, are snapped together in the picture, so the moment of the clack is recorded on both the picture and the sound. When sound and picture are recorded separately, editors use that shared cue to match them.

cards.headline: The whole chapter in one scene

On paper, each screenplay page is about a minute, and storyboards and shot lists plan every shot. title: What Editing Does
objective: After this level you can explain how an editor chooses, orders and trims shots, from cutting film by hand to editing software.
summary: An editor reviews the footage, picks the best takes, orders and trims them. Editors once spliced celluloid on machines like the 1924 Moviola; since the 1990s, nonlinear software jumps to any frame.

cards.headline: A film gets made three times, and the last time, no camera rolls.
cards.body: A common saying holds that a film is made three times: when the script is written, when it's shot, and again in the editing. When the cameras stop, the movie still doesn't exist. What exists is a heap of takes, waiting for someone to choose. Who is that someone, and what are they actually doing?

cards.headline: Choose, order, trim
cards.body: That someone is the editor. An editor reviews all the footage, selects the best take of each shot and puts them in order, working from a rough cut toward a fine cut. Level 1 gave you the rest of the job: trimming and piecing the footage together, judging exactly how long every shot should last. No wonder editing, cutting and montage are often used as words for the same thing. The story you watch is the one the editor found in the heap.

cards.headline: Scissors, splices and the Moviola
cards.body: For most of film history, editing was physical. Editors cut strips of celluloid and spliced them together, on machines that ran footage from the start of a take to its end. In 1924, Iwan Serrurier's Moviola was adapted for editing: an upright machine with a single screen that let an editor watch film while cutting it. Want a moment near the end of a take? Scroll through every frame before it.

cards.headline: Jump anywhere: editing goes digital
cards.body: Since the 1990s, editors have worked on digital nonlinear systems such as Avid. They don't cut film at all: they sit at a keyboard, and the software jumps instantly to any point in the footage. That's what nonlinear means: no more rolling past every frame to reach the one you want. The choices are the same as ever. Getting to them is much faster.

title: Invisible Editing
objective: After this level you can explain continuity editing and the match on action, which hide cuts so a scene feels unbroken.
summary: Continuity editing, classical Hollywood's 'invisible editing', matches direction, position and time across cuts. A match on action carries a movement across the cut.

cards.headline: A scene is full of cuts. So why doesn't it feel chopped up?
cards.body: A scene you watch is really a string of separate shots, joined by cuts. Yet a character crosses a room and it feels like one smooth moment, in one place, at one time. Somebody worked hard to keep it that way. Here's the system behind it.

cards.headline: Hollywood's invisible style
cards.body: From the 1930s to the 1950s, classical Hollywood's dominant style is sometimes called invisible editing, because its cuts are so unobtrusive. Its formal name is continuity editing: a system of cutting that keeps the action clear and continuous by matching screen direction, positions and time from shot to shot. It backs up an assumption you make without thinking: that space and time run on unbroken across every cut.

cards.headline: Cut in the middle of a move
cards.body: A favorite place to hide a cut is inside a movement. In a match on action, a movement begun in one shot is picked up where it left off in the next. A hand reaches for a cup, cut, and a closer shot finishes the reach. The movement stitches the two shots together, so you read one continuous gesture instead of a join.

cards.headline: The doorway that joins two places
cards.body: D. W. Griffith used the trick in the films he made at Biograph from 1908 to 1913. A character walks into a doorway outdoors, and in the next shot enters an interior built as a set. The outside and the inside were filmed in different places, but the matched step through the door makes them one house. The door is the stitch.

title: The 180-Degree Rule
objective: After this level you can explain how the 180-degree rule keeps characters on the same sides of the screen so viewers stay oriented.
summary: An establishing shot lays out a scene. The 180-degree rule keeps the camera on one side of the axis of action, so characters stay on their sides of the frame; crossing it needs a reestablishing shot.

cards.headline: Film two friends from the wrong spot, and they seem to swap seats.
cards.body: Picture two friends in a diner booth, one on the left, one on the right. The film cuts from one face to the other and back. Nobody moves, yet one careless camera position can put the friend on the left suddenly on the right, and your sense of the room flips. Filmmakers have a rule to stop that.

mascot.line: Keep this: draw the line between the characters, keep the camera on one side, and left stays left.

cards.headline: Draw a line between them
cards.body: Imagine a line running between the two characters. Filmmakers call it the axis of action, and the 180-degree rule keeps the camera on one side of it: anywhere in that half circle, but never across. Every shot then keeps each character in the same area of the frame. The friend on the left stays on the left, cut after cut, so the screen's left-right geography never flips.

cards.headline: First, the map: the establishing shot
cards.body: Before the close shots begin, a scene often opens wide. An establishing shot, usually a distant framing, shows how the important people, objects and setting are laid out. It hands you the map of the room. After that, the 180-degree rule keeps the map from flipping while the camera moves in close.

cards.headline: Crossing the line
cards.body: The line can be crossed, but usually only when a reestablishing shot smooths the change, showing the space again so you can redraw your map. Editors can also break continuity on purpose, to undermine your sense of the space. Cross the line by accident and you feel lost. Cross it deliberately, and that lost feeling can become the point.

title: Shot, Reverse Shot
objective: After this level you can explain how shot, reverse shot and eyeline matches build a conversation out of separate shots.
summary: Shot/reverse shot alternates between characters in a conversation, joined by eyeline matches: a look off-screen, then what is seen. Because it is assembled, the editor shapes the performances.

cards.headline: In many film conversations, you see one face at a time.
cards.body: One face talks. Cut. The other face listens. Cut back. You feel as if you're sitting at the table with them, but you're watching separate shots taking turns. How does a string of single faces add up to two people talking to each other?

cards.headline: Taking turns: shot, reverse shot
cards.body: The pattern is called shot/reverse shot: two or more shots edited together that alternate between characters, typically in a conversation. Each character is often shown in a close-up of their own, and the cuts usually follow the flow of the dialogue. It's like watching a tennis rally from the stands: your attention passes back and forth with the ball.

cards.headline: Where they look tells you where they are
cards.body: What glues the separate close-ups together is the eyeline match. One shot shows a person looking off-screen in one direction; the next shows what they see. Direction matters: if she looks left, the next shot implies she's off-screen to the right, looking at him. Get the eyelines right and two faces, shown separately, seem to meet across the table.

cards.headline: The editor shapes the acting, too
cards.body: Because the conversation is assembled, the editor gets a say in it. Staying on the speaker gives a line one tone; cutting to the listener's reaction gives the same line another. Editors trim the ends of shots so an actor seems to jump in on someone's line, or draw out a pause. Viewers credit the actors with much of what the editor built.

title: Cross-Cutting
objective: After this level you can explain how cutting between two lines of action happening at once builds suspense.
summary: Crosscutting alternates lines of action in different places at once. Griffith's rescues, as in The Girl and Her Trust (1912), built suspense with ever shorter shots.

cards.headline: A robber escapes, a rescuer gives chase, and you get to watch both.
cards.body: Show only the robbers and you'd wonder where help was. Show only the rescuer and you'd wonder where the robbers were. Cut back and forth between them, and you know exactly how close the rescue is, and how far it still has to go. That knowledge is what builds suspense.

cards.headline: Two places, one clock
cards.body: Cutting between lines of action is called crosscutting, or parallel editing: shots of two or more actions, in different places and usually happening at the same time, alternate on screen, linking them. You met an early example in Level 8, when Porter cut back and forth between the tied-up telegraph operator and the bandits on the train. Each line of action makes you think about the other.

cards.headline: The ride to the rescue
cards.body: D. W. Griffith became famous for crosscutting in the last-minute rescues that climax his films. In The Girl and Her Trust (1912), robbers escape with the heroine on a railroad pump car while the hero chases them by train. Griffith cuts from one to the other and back. Pump car, train, pump car, train: the gap is closing, but is it closing fast enough?

cards.headline: Shorter shots, faster pulse
cards.body: Intercutting the two lines of action creates the suspense. Then Griffith sped it up by shortening the shots as the chase went on, so the cuts come quicker and quicker until the lines meet. The pace of the cutting becomes your pulse. Crosscutting became a foundation of storytelling on film.

title: Jump Cuts and Match Cuts
objective: After this level you can tell a jump cut from a match cut and explain the effect each has on a viewer.
summary: A jump cut leaves out part of an action so time visibly skips, as in Godard's Breathless (1960). A match cut joins shots with matching shapes, as when a bone becomes a satellite in 2001.

cards.headline: Some cuts hide. These two want you to notice them.
cards.body: Level 32's invisible editing works hard to hide every join. But filmmakers also have cuts that do the opposite. One makes time skip like a scratched record. The other makes two different things rhyme. Here's what each one does to you.

cards.headline: The jump cut: time skips
cards.body: A jump cut leaves out part of an action, so the picture visibly jumps: a person is here, then suddenly a little further along. Nothing hides the gap. Jean-Luc Godard's Breathless (1960) used jump cuts that left out parts of the action, and French New Wave films made them a hallmark of their style.

cards.headline: Why a jump cut feels jumpy
cards.body: Continuity editing supports your sense that space and time run on unbroken. A jump cut breaks that promise on purpose. It breaks with mainstream storytelling and reminds you that someone assembled what you're watching. Used well, the jolt can also suggest a character's restless thoughts.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. A jump cut breaks time; a match cut links two shapes. One jolts, the other rhymes.

cards.headline: The match cut: a visual rhyme
cards.body: A match cut, or graphic match, joins two shots with strongly similar compositions, matching shape or color, to smooth a transition or suggest a comparison. The famous one: in 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), a man-ape tosses a bone into the air, and a single cut turns it into an orbiting satellite. One shape carries you from prehistory to the space age.

title: The Kuleshov Effect
objective: After this level you can explain how the Kuleshov experiment showed that viewers read an actor's face from the shots around it.
summary: Kuleshov cut a neutral face against soup, a child or a corpse, and viewers saw hunger, tenderness or grief. The footage is lost, but a 2016 study found some such effect.

cards.headline: The same face, the same shot, and viewers saw different feelings.
cards.body: An actor stares ahead with a neutral expression. Put that shot after a bowl of soup, and viewers see hunger. Put it next to something else, and they see something else. The face never changed. So who was doing the acting?

cards.headline: Kuleshov's experiment
cards.body: Lev Kuleshov, a Soviet film theorist, taught that montage, the cutting and joining of shots, was the most important part of filmmaking. To show it, he cut an actor's neutral face against different shots, such as soup, a child or a corpse. Viewers read the same face as hungry, tender or grieving. The lesson: a shot has two values, what it shows by itself and what it gains next to another shot.

cards.headline: Why it works: you follow the look
cards.body: The effect runs on Level 34's eyeline logic. You take the face to be looking at whatever comes next. A 2024 study describes the sequence as a glance shot, the face, followed by an object shot, the thing seen. Your mind supplies the feeling that would connect the two.

cards.headline: A famous experiment with missing evidence
cards.body: Here's the catch. The original footage is lost, and tellings of the experiment differ, even about which shots were used. It's doubtful it worked exactly as Kuleshov claimed: the face came from an existing film and likely held an ambiguous expression. So researchers tested it again. After conflicting results, a 2016 study with 36 participants found that some sort of Kuleshov effect does exist.

title: Sound in the Story, Sound for Us
objective: After this level you can tell diegetic sound, which the characters can hear, from non-diegetic sound, which only the audience hears.
summary: Diegetic sound comes from the story world, so characters could hear it; non-diegetic sound, like most background music, is only for the audience.

cards.headline: The music swells. Why doesn't the hero hear it and run?
cards.body: The strings shriek, the drums pound, and the character on screen strolls on, calm as ever. The music isn't in their world. It's in yours. Film sound comes in two kinds, and the difference is simply who can hear it.

cards.headline: The story world and its sounds
cards.body: Film scholars call the world of the story its diegesis: the objects, events, places and characters in it, including things you infer but never see. Diegetic sound, whether a voice, music or a sound effect, is presented as coming from a source inside that world: a character talking, a band playing at a party, a radio on the kitchen counter.

mascot.line: Keep this test: could anyone in the scene hear it? Yes, diegetic. No, it plays only for you.

cards.headline: Sound just for you
cards.body: Non-diegetic sound comes from outside the story world. Most background music is non-diegetic: you hear it, the characters don't. There's no orchestra hiding behind the sofa. So the test is simple. Could someone in the scene hear it, if they listened? Yes means diegetic. No means it's only for you.

cards.headline: Sounds inside a head
cards.body: Some sounds sit in between. Internal diegetic sound comes from inside a character's mind, such as their thoughts or sounds they imagine. It belongs to the story world, but no one else in the scene can hear it. It's a way of putting you inside one person's head.

title: Foley and Sound Design
objective: After this level you can explain how Foley artists and sound designers create footsteps, punches and whole worlds of sound after filming.
summary: Early talkie mics mainly caught dialogue, so Foley artists add action sounds later, in sync. In 1979 Walter Murch became film's first credited Sound Designer.

cards.headline: Many footsteps you hear in films were made later, by someone else.
cards.body: An actor strides down a hallway and every step clicks. But the microphones of the early talkies were built mainly for dialogue, so sounds like those steps had to be added at a later step. The people who add them are artists who create sounds for on-screen actions, from walking to a creaking door. Meet them.

cards.headline: Why sounds get added later
cards.body: When talkies arrived, microphones were designed mainly to pick up dialogue. Other sounds had to be added afterwards to make the film believable. At Universal in the late 1920s, Jack Foley added clapping, laughter and other sounds to Show Boat as the film ran in real time. He almost single-handedly built the craft, and it still carries his name: Foley.

cards.headline: A stage full of shoes and lettuce
cards.body: Foley artists create sounds for specific actions on screen: someone walking, a sword fight, a creaking door. They work on a Foley stage full of props, such as shoes of all kinds, watching the scene on a large screen so every sound lands in sync. The prop only has to sound right. For Titanic, the crackle of frost was frozen lettuce.

cards.headline: The sound designer: one plan for every sound
cards.body: In 1979, Francis Ford Coppola gave Walter Murch the credit Sound Designer for Apocalypse Now, the first use of that title in film. Murch oversaw the film's overall sound concept: dialogue, sound effects, Foley and the final mix. Footsteps, explosions and silences all answered to one plan.

title: The Talkies Arrive
objective: After this level you can explain why The Jazz Singer's synchronized sound in 1927 upended Hollywood so quickly, and what it cost silent stars and cameras.
summary: Warner Brothers bet on Vitaphone; The Jazz Singer's 1927 success, with sound for only a quarter of it, pushed Hollywood into talkies within about 15 months and locked cameras in booths.

cards.headline: In 1927, a mostly silent movie ended the silent era.
cards.body: The Jazz Singer had recorded sound for its songs and some conversations, about a quarter of the film. The rest played like any silent picture. Yet its success pushed all of Hollywood into talking pictures. Why did a part-talkie change everything, and what did the switch cost?

cards.headline: A small studio's big bet
cards.body: The bet came from Warner Brothers, then a minor studio. It bought Vitaphone, Western Electric's sound-on-disc system, which played a recorded disc in step with the film, and debuted it in 1926 with Don Juan. The Jazz Singer followed in 1927, and its phenomenal success virtually ensured the industry's switch to sound. Its star, Al Jolson, performed in blackface, a stage tradition in which white performers caricatured Black people, built on racial derision.

cards.headline: The camera goes into an icebox
cards.body: Sound changed how films were shot. Early microphones had a very limited range, so actors spoke toward them and stood practically still. Cameras were shut inside soundproof glass booths, nicknamed iceboxes because they were hot and stuffy, so the camera couldn't tilt or roll on a dolly. That's why so many early talkies look stiff. By 1931 studios had switched to lightweight soundproof camera housings called blimps, and the camera moved again.

cards.headline: Fifteen months, and a test for every voice
cards.body: Hollywood converted to sound in less than 15 months, between late 1927 and 1929, and studios and theaters had to be completely reequipped. Actors faced a new test: their voices. Some silent stars' careers did not survive the switch: the German actor Emil Jannings, whose heavy accent had never been heard on a silent screen, had to leave Hollywood and went back to making films in Germany.

title: The Big Studios
objective: After this level you can explain why the major studios owned the whole chain, from making films to the theaters that showed them.
summary: By 1930 eight studios made 95 percent of American films. The five majors owned the whole chain, from production to theaters, and block booking pushed their films into the rest.

cards.headline: What if a bakery owned every café that sold its bread?
cards.body: It would never worry about shelf space. Hollywood's biggest studios worked like that: they made films, rented them out to theaters and owned many of the theaters that showed them. Why would a movie studio want to own the whole chain?

cards.headline: Five majors, three minors
cards.body: By 1930, eight studios made 95 percent of American films. Five majors, MGM, Paramount, Warner Brothers, Twentieth Century-Fox and RKO, controlled all three links: production (making films), distribution (renting them to theaters) and exhibition (showing them). Universal, Columbia and United Artists made and distributed films but didn't own the big theater chains.

cards.headline: Why buy the theaters?
cards.body: Through the 1920s, Paramount, MGM and other studios bought up chains of first-run theaters. After that, Britannica says, the majors are best seen as theater chains that made features, shorts, cartoons and newsreels to fill their own houses. Owning the screens meant every film a studio made had a place to play.

cards.headline: Films sold by the block
cards.body: Theaters the studios didn't own still needed their films, and the studios set the terms. Under block booking, a theater could license the film it wanted only if it also took other films the distributor released in that period. Want this season's big picture? Take the package.

title: The Star System
objective: After this level you can explain why studios signed actors to long contracts and carefully built their public images.
summary: Studios first kept actors anonymous, then found that stars sold films. They built stars' images with publicity and bound them with seven-year contracts, which Olivia de Havilland challenged.

cards.headline: The first film fans didn't know their favorite's name.
cards.body: Early studios kept their actors anonymous. So audiences who loved Florence Lawrence knew her only as the Biograph Girl, named after her studio. How did a nameless face become the most valuable thing a studio owned?

cards.headline: A name worth selling
cards.body: In 1910 Carl Laemmle hired Lawrence for his new company, the Independent Motion Picture Company, and promoted her by name. She became one of the first movie stars. The studios learned the lesson fast: the film star was perhaps the most important development in film advertising. A new title is a stranger; a star is someone you already want to see.

cards.headline: Stars were built, not born
cards.body: So the studios manufactured stars. Publicists wrote polished life stories and fed photos and 'intimate' confessions to fan magazines. Contracts carried morality clauses, giving the studio a say over how a star behaved off screen too. The star you read about was partly a studio product, just like the films.

cards.headline: Seven years, and then some
cards.body: The standard star contract ran seven years. Olivia de Havilland tested it. In the mid-1940s she won a precedent-setting case against Warner Brothers, which had tacked a six-month penalty onto her seven-year contract. Free at last, she took more challenging roles and won Academy Awards for To Each His Own and The Heiress.
